value.overview: The Little Blue Heron (Egretta caerulea) is a medium-sized wading bird found from the southern United States through Central America and the Caribbean to much of South America. Adults have slate-blue bodies, violet-maroon heads and necks, and dark-tipped, pale gray bills. Young birds are mostly white and can resemble Snowy Egrets. The species usually hunts alone in shallow wetlands and often nests in mixed colonies with other herons and egrets.
value.classification: The Little Blue Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Egretta caerulea.
value.identification: Adults are about 60 centimeters long, with long legs, a long pointed bill, and dark blue-gray plumage. The head and neck may appear purplish, especially in good light. The bill is pale gray or bluish with a darker tip, and the legs are dark. Immatures are largely white during their first year, often showing pale greenish legs and a gray-and-black bill. Their slow wingbeats and slim shape help distinguish them from larger herons.
value.rangeHabitat: The Little Blue Heron ranges from the southeastern United States and Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in the lowlands of both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, where it uses freshwater marshes, ponds, lakes, slow rivers, rice fields, mudflats, estuaries, mangroves, salt ponds, and other shallow wetlands. It is commonly associated with open wetland edges and sheltered roosting or nesting vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: The species is resident in much of the tropics, while northern populations migrate southward after breeding. In Costa Rica it is primarily a passage migrant and winter visitor, with some individuals remaining during the breeding season; it is generally not considered a regular breeding resident there.
value.breeding: Little Blue Herons usually breed colonially, often alongside Great Egrets, Snowy Egrets, Tricolored Herons, and other waterbirds. They build a platform of sticks in trees, shrubs, mangroves, or dense wetland vegetation near feeding areas. Both adults incubate the eggs and care for the young. Northern populations commonly lay about three to six eggs, while clutches in Central America are often smaller. Reliable sources do not indicate that Costa Rica supports a major regular breeding population.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, frogs, tadpoles, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other small aquatic animals. The heron usually walks slowly through shallow water or stands motionless before making a quick strike with its bill. It may forage along muddy margins, flooded fields, streams, ponds, estuaries, and mangrove channels. Individuals commonly feed alone, although several may gather where prey become concentrated.
value.behavior: Little Blue Herons are generally quiet and solitary while feeding, and they often occur singly or in pairs rather than in large feeding flocks. They may congregate with other waders at roosts, nesting colonies, and rich feeding sites. Adults fly with slow, deliberate wingbeats and the neck folded back. Young birds remain white for much of their first year, a coloration that may reduce aggression from adult herons in mixed colonies.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although the species remains widespread and numerous enough to be classified as Least Concern.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss, drainage, pollution, and degradation of wetlands; disturbance of nesting colonies and communal roosts; removal of wetland vegetation; and reduced availability of shallow feeding habitat. Declines have been reported in parts of North America, so continued protection of wetlands and breeding colonies is important even though the global assessment is Least Concern.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore marshes, ponds, mangroves, estuaries, and other shallow wetlands. Avoid disturbing nesting colonies and roosts, especially during the breeding season, and support conservation of Costa Rica’s wetland reserves and coastal habitats. Reducing pesticide and chemical runoff, keeping dogs and people away from sensitive colonies, and reporting sightings through established bird-monitoring programs can also help improve knowledge and conservation planning.
